HIGH-LEVEL ARCHITECTURAL REQUIREMENTS (Section 7) Five categories of requirements: - REQ-ML-COR: Enablers for correlation — support correlation of data from multiple sources, multiple technologies, distributed instantiation - REQ-ML-DEP: Enablers for deployment — define interaction points, support split/combined deployments, flexible placement, plug-and-play data sources - REQ-ML-INT: Interface-related — support model transfer, data transfer for training, standard APIs, data sharing mechanisms - REQ-ML-SPEC: Declarative specifications — standard ML application representation, specification of data sources/model repos/targets/constraints, flexible split, third-party specifications - REQ-ML-MNG: Management of ML functionalities — model selection, training/updates, monitoring, orchestration, flexible chaining 6. ITU AI for Good Sandbox Network - Summary 1. OVERVIEW The ITU AI for Good Sandbox is a distributed, standards-based platform that lowers barriers to AI research, experimentation, and innovation. It provides cloud computing resources, datasets, and tools for AI experimentation aligned with ITU-T standards. 2. KEY CAPABILITIES - Cloud credit support for AI experimentation projects - Access to computing resources (GPU/CPU) for model training - Hosting environment for AI models and datasets - Sandbox environments for testing AI solutions in controlled settings - Integration with ITU-T standards for interoperability 3. SANDBOX NETWORK VISION - Distributed network of sandboxes across regions and countries - Standards-based (ITU-T Y.3172) pipeline architecture - Enables collaboration across countries and domains - Bridges gap between open science, research, and standardization - Local deployment capability for data sovereignty 4. USE CASES SUPPORTED - AI model training and validation - Policy impact simulation and extrapolation - Domain-specific AI testing (healthcare, agriculture, disaster management) - Cross-domain correlation analysis - GenAI content generation and evaluation 5. RELEVANCE TO ITU AI READINESS FRAMEWORK - The Sandbox is the primary hosting environment for the AI-RE Toolkit - Dimension 10 (AI & Policies): Sandbox provides simulated timelines for policy what-if analysis - Dimension 11 (AI for Inclusion): Sandbox hosts digital twins and simulation environments - Factor 6 (Sandbox): Directly maps to the sandbox environments factor - Knowledge Base is hosted within the Sandbox infrastructure - Multiple toolkit instances can run in parallel, connected to the Sandbox for KB record transfer 6. PLUGFEST INTEGRATION - Cloud credits provided to selected Plugfest projects - Projects validated in sandbox environments - Results feed back into the AI Readiness Framework dimensions and metrics

retrieved.text: Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect. Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake shall disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.

High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use. Human oversight shall aim to prevent or minimise the risks to health, safety or fundamental rights that may emerge when a high-risk AI system is used.

Annex III lists high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2). Point 5 covers access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits. Point 5(a) covers AI systems intended to be used by public authorities or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, as well as to grant, reduce, revoke, or reclaim such benefits and services.

The Generative AI profile treats prompt injection as a risk to systems that read untrusted text. An untrusted message can carry an instruction that tries to override the system's task, for example by telling the system to disclose a record or to ignore its policy. A pre-processor screen should flag that pattern before the model acts on it. A canary string planted only in the untrusted message is a test that the instruction was not copied into an action.

The Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI was published in 2024 by the AI Verify Foundation and the Infocomm Media Development Authority. URL: https://aiverifyfoundation.sg/resources/model-ai-governance-framework-for-generative-ai/ The framework text is not reproduced. This briefing is original and is licensed CC0.

The framework also expects testing against abusive prompts and a way to report incidents when a generative system states a fact or a rule it should not state. Those controls sit beside accountability: the organisation that deploys the system remains responsible for the reply.

The profile also treats confabulation, sometimes called hallucination, as a risk that a generative system will state a rule or a fee that no instrument contains. Content provenance and a human check are the controls the profile points to before such a statement is shown to the public.
